title: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode I
statement:
Choose 5 positions `i0 < i1 < i2 < i3 < i4` of `nums` and read `seq = [nums[i0], nums[i1], nums[i2], nums[i3], nums[i4]]` in that order. The choice counts when the middle element `seq[2]` is the **unique mode** of `seq`: it occurs in `seq` strictly more times than every other value that occurs in `seq`.

Return the number of choices of 5 positions that count. Different sets of positions are counted separately even when they give the same values. The number can be very large, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Listing every 5-element subsequence is O(n⁵). Instead, fix the middle position `middle` with value `x`: the other four elements are two from its left and two from its right. Whether `x` is the unique mode depends only on how many of those four are also `x`:

- none: `x` occurs once and cannot beat everything else (bad);
- exactly one: `x` occurs twice, which is bad exactly when another value occurs twice or more among the other three;
- two or more: `x` occurs at least three times out of five (good).

So count all choices and subtract the two bad kinds, using only how often each value occurs on each side.

## Approach

1. Give each distinct value an id in `ids`. `left[v]` and `right[v]` count value `v` before and after the middle; everything starts in `right`.
2. For each `middle`, take its element out of `right`; `leftOther` and `rightOther` count the elements on each side that are not `x`.
3. Start `good` at all choices, `pairs(middle) * pairs(n - 1 - middle)`, minus those with no other `x`, `pairs(leftOther) * pairs(rightOther)`.
4. One more `x` on the left (`left[x]` ways) leaves one non-`x` pick on the left and two on the right. For each other value `v`, subtract the cases where both right picks are `v` (`leftOther * pairs(right[v])`) and where the left pick and exactly one right pick are `v` (`left[v] * right[v] * (rightOther - right[v])`). Mirror this for one more `x` on the right.
5. Add `good` to `answer` modulo 10^9 + 7 and move `x` into `left`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]` holds one value, so `leftOther = rightOther = 0` and nothing is subtracted. `middle = 2` gives `pairs(2) * pairs(3) = 3`, `middle = 3` gives `pairs(3) * pairs(2) = 3`, and every other middle lacks two elements on one side, so `answer = 6`. (In Example 2, at `middle = 2` the term for value 3 removes the tie `[1, 2, 2, 3, 3]` from 3 choices, leaving 2.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n · d) for d distinct values: each middle visits every value id once, at most 10^6 steps.
- Space: O(d) for `ids`, `left` and `right`.

## Pitfalls

- A middle value that occurs once is never a unique mode, even when all five values differ.
- With two copies of `x`, a rival occurring three times is bad too; `leftOther * pairs(right[v])` already includes the left pick being `v`.
- Skip `v === x`: copies of `x` are never rivals.
- A middle's count reaches about 1.5 · 10^10, still exact in a JavaScript number; apply the modulo when adding to `answer`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pairs(k)` | k choose 2 |
| `ids` | map from each distinct value to a small id |
| `left`, `right` | how often each value id occurs before and after the middle |
| `middle` | index of the middle element |
| `x` | id of `nums[middle]` |
| `leftOther`, `rightOther` | elements before and after the middle that are not `x` |
| `good` | choices around this middle where `x` is the unique mode |
| `v` | id of another value |
| `answer` | total so far, modulo `MOD` |
